ACLED’s Somalia Analyst, Mohamed Daud, comments on the growing political standoff over Somalia’s electoral system, the risk of renewed armed conflict, and the challenges of holding direct elections. 23 November 2026 On this page Author Mohamed Daud Ismail Senior Research Assistant On 17 November 2026, Somalia's federal government accused the United Arab Emirates of interfering in its internal affairs and undermining the country's sovereignty, territorial integrity, and national unity. The government called for the expulsion of the UAE ambassador and urged Abu Dhabi to channel all dealings with Somalia through the federal government. The UAE rejected any accusations, arguing the government was putting personal interests ahead of the country’s national interests, and said its embassy in Somalia had been closed since January 2026. ACLED’s Somalia Analyst, Mohamed Daud, said: “The UAE maintains ties with several regional administrations in Somalia that are at odds with the federal government in Mogadishu, including Jubaland, Puntland, Somaliland, and the former Southwest administration. It also supports armed movements in the Hiiraan region of the Hirshabelle administration. These relationships have fuelled tensions with Mogadishu, which accuses Abu Dhabi of backing regional administrations that challenge the federal government. “The UAE's ties with these local administrations are driven in part by economic interests but also by counter-insurgency operations against Al Shabaab and Islamic State (IS) militants in Southern-central and Northern Somalia, respectively. The UAE has invested heavily in the seaports in Berbera and Bosaso and has modern military bases in both cities in Somaliland and Puntland. “Since January 2025, ACLED has recorded 43 UAE airstrikes against Islamic State and Al Shabaab in Cal Miskat and Golis mountain ranges of Somalia's Bari region in Puntland. The majority of these incidents occurred in February 2025, when Puntland intensified operations targeting IS. “Relations between Mogadishu and Abu Dhabi have further deteriorated after national election talks between the government and the opposition alliance failed to open on 14 November 2026, following a boycott by the main opposition alliance. The government has previously accused the UAE of supporting members of the opposition alliance. Disputes over power-sharing arrangements and electoral reforms have long been a source of tension in Somalia, underpinning broader disagreements over political authority and governance. “By directly challenging the UAE's ties with sub-national entities, the government risks further straining its already fragile relations with key federal member states and Somaliland, deepening political instability across Somalia. Mogadishu’s framing of these partnerships as violations of national sovereignty could also exacerbate disputes over regional autonomy and undermine security cooperation against insurgent groups. Meanwhile, the opposition alliance has interpreted the government's rhetoric as an attempt to consolidate power ahead of election negotiations and reaffirmed its decision to boycott all consultative talks until key governance and electoral reform concerns are addressed. “The move could push the UAE closer to Hargeysa and could make it the second country, after Israel, to recognize Somaliland as a sovereign state.” Want to know more? On November 17, 2026, Somalia called for the expulsion of the UAE ambassador and insisted that all dealings with the UAE be conducted through the federal government. The UAE denied these accusations, asserting that Somalia's government was prioritizing personal interests over national ones. The significance of healthcare, education and water projects extends beyond the value of the funding allocated to them to encompass their capacity to provide communities with sustained services. SR Staff Reporter · Garowe Online 23 Nov 2026 · 22:43 · 4 min read Hospitals providing free medical treatment, educational and water projects spanning more than a decade, and Somali and regional commendations for the UAE’s humanitarian support to a country grappling with accumulated development challenges. In the Somali capital, Mogadishu, where years of conflict and weak infrastructure have posed significant obstacles to accessing healthcare services, Sheikh Zayed Hospital stands as a tangible example of the humanitarian projects implemented by the United Arab Emirates to support the Somali population. Opened in 2015 and reopened following comprehensive renovation works in February 2024, the hospital provides patients with free medical services and medication in a country where healthcare costs remain a barrier for many families. The hospital represents just one aspect of a broader UAE assistance effort in Somalia, which over more than a decade has encompassed healthcare and education projects, well drilling and water provision, as well as food relief programmes and assistance to displaced families. Official data indicate that assistance provided to Somalia between 2010 and March 2020 amounted to approximately AED 1.2 billion, distributed across several sectors, including education, healthcare, water and social services. Sheikh Zayed Hospital: Free Healthcare in the Heart of Mogadishu In April 2018, the US-based Atlantic Council published an analysis of UAE-Somalia relations, noting that the UAE government and its charitable institutions had funded numerous humanitarian projects, including Sheikh Zayed Hospital in Mogadishu. The centre explained that the hospital, which opened in 2015, provided free treatment to hundreds of patients daily. This reference is particularly significant because it appeared in an analysis published by an international research institution examining relations between the two countries within a complex political context, rather than merely presenting official UAE data. On 2 February 2024, the hospital entered a new phase with its reopening following rehabilitation works and the installation of modern medical equipment. The ceremony was attended by Somali Prime Minister Hamza Abdi Barre and UAE Ambassador Ahmed Juma Al Rumaithi. The development works covered the emergency, general surgery, internal medicine, paediatrics, dentistry, obstetrics and gynaecology, dermatology, and ear, nose and throat departments, in addition to medical imaging services. According to the official statement issued by the UAE Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Somali prime minister praised bilateral relations and cooperation between the two countries during the reopening ceremony and expressed his appreciation for the UAE’s efforts to support Somalia. This position echoed earlier remarks by Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, who, during the inauguration of a UAE-funded training centre in May 2015, commended the assistance Abu Dhabi had provided to his country throughout years of political and economic crises. Education and Water: Investing in the Foundations of Life Beyond healthcare institutions, UAE projects extended to sectors addressing the everyday needs of Somali communities. According to data published by the UAE Ministry of Foreign Affairs in April 2020, support allocated to education amounted to approximately AED 132 million between 2010 and March 2020, compared with AED 59 million for healthcare and AED 160 million for water and public health services. The interventions included the construction and equipping of educational and healthcare facilities, well drilling and support for social programmes across various parts of Somalia. In a country where a large proportion of the population depends on pastoralism and agriculture, the importance of providing water extends beyond domestic consumption to protecting livelihoods and reducing the need for families to flee their homes during periods of drought. Reports by the United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF) illustrate the scale of the ongoing challenges in this sector. In its Humanitarian Situation Report for the first half of 2024, the organisation stated that it had helped approximately 729,000 people gain access to emergency water supplies as part of its broader humanitarian response in Somalia. Commendation from the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation UAE assistance to Somalia received official commendation from the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) during the 51st session of its Council of Foreign Ministers in 2025. In its resolution concerning Somalia, the organisation praised the UAE’s ongoing humanitarian efforts, noting that more than $200 million in assistance had been provided since the beginning of 2023. The resolution affirmed that the support included urgent food and medical supplies, as well as the drilling of wells to provide clean water and mitigate the effects of drought and the humanitarian crisis. The organisation described these interventions as reflecting the UAE’s commitment to supporting the Somali people in difficult humanitarian circumstances. This commendation stands as one of the most prominent official regional acknowledgements of UAE assistance. From Relief to Sustainable Services The significance of healthcare, education and water projects extends beyond the value of the funding allocated to them to encompass their capacity to provide communities with sustained services. A hospital that continues to receive patients years after its opening offers a model fundamentally different from a relief shipment consumed within days or weeks. Similarly, wells and educational facilities can deliver a more lasting impact when supported by maintenance, management and operational funding. In Somalia, where climate, economic and security crises intersect, the sustainability of essential services remains a challenge requiring cooperation between local authorities, international partners and humanitarian organisations. Notably, Sheikh Zayed Hospital in Mogadishu, which reopened in February 2024 after renovations, offers free medical services to a population facing healthcare access challenges. embassy in Mogadishu and withdrawn its diplomats in January 2026, after Somalia cancelled all its agreements with the UAE. The UAE has long denied meddling in Somalia, according to Reuters. SR Staff Reporter · Garowe Online 23 Nov 2026 · 22:25 · 5 min read Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud has chosen to escalate tensions with the United Arab Emirates at a time when he is facing multiple crises at home. The UAE asserts that he is attempting to drag it into internal power struggles in Mogadishu. In a televised speech on November 17, 2026, Mohamud accused the UAE of interfering in Somalia’s internal affairs, funding political divisions and supporting armed militias. He also said the UAE had made deals with regional administrations over the ports of Berbera, Bosaso and Kismayo without the federal government’s consent, Addis Standard reported . The three ports are in Somaliland, Puntland and Jubaland, which are all in dispute with Mogadishu. On November 19, Somalia’s cabinet ordered the UAE ambassador to leave within 72 hours and recalled its own ambassador from Abu Dhabi. The UAE Ministry of Foreign Affairs responded the same day. It condemned what it called the Somali government’s “escalatory and hostile approach” and said it regretted Mogadishu’s attempts to bring its internal power struggles into relations between the two countries. The ministry said Somalia’s “irresponsible positions” were damaging those relations. The ministry also said the UAE had closed its embassy in Mogadishu and withdrawn its diplomats in January 2026, after Somalia cancelled all its agreements with the UAE. The UAE has long denied meddling in Somalia, according to Reuters. Two days before Mohamud’s speech, Mohamed Osman, argued in a blog post hosted by The Times of Israel that the federal government blames Ethiopia, Kenya, or the UAE for Somalia’s political turmoil. But the forces paralyzing the state today are homegrown: domestic institutional failures, elite power struggles, and federal bargains that were never settled. Outside actors may exploit these divisions, but they did not create the constitutional, judicial, or federal breakdowns at the heart of the crisis. A Presidency in Crisis: Mohamud Faces Growing Opposition to His Rule The dispute with the UAE comes during a political crisis that began in May 2026, when Mohamud’s term was first due to end, according to an analysis Chatham House published on October 16. Mohamud was elected in May 2022. On March 4, 2026, parliament voted to change the constitution and extend the terms of the president and lawmakers from four years to five, Reuters reported. The vote pushed elections back by a year. The amendments also let citizens elect members of the lower house directly and give the federal government more power over revenue, elections and intervention in member states, Al Jazeera reported . Parliament still elects the president. Puntland and Jubaland reject the changes, according to Al Jazeera. So do Abdiaziz Hassan Mohamed Laftagareen, the former president of South West State, and the Somali Future Council, an opposition coalition that includes former presidents and prime ministers. On October 15, the electoral commission set parliamentary elections for April 15, 2027, and the presidential election for May 15, 2027. Opposition leaders rejected the timetable as one-sided, Garowe Online reported. Chatham House said the crisis had led to fierce clashes in Mogadishu and in Baidoa, in South West State. It also said Turkey is seen as backing the federal government while the UAE has relations with the opposition state administrations. Federal forces took Baidoa on March 30, and Laftagareen then resigned, according to the Associated Press. On September 28, thousands of fighters loyal to him entered the city, and fighter jets and drones were reported in the fighting, according to Al Jazeera. Judicial Showdown Threatens Mohamud's Political Legitimacy On November 5, 2026, the Supreme Court ruled that Mohamud’s term had ended on May 15 and parliament’s on April 14. It ordered political leaders to agree on an electoral framework within 30 days and hold elections within 90 days. The five judges found that the extension from four to five years could not apply to officials already in office. Former President Sharif Sheikh Ahmed brought the case. In a separate decision that day, the court declared invalid Mohamud’s dismissal of Chief Justice Bashe Yusuf Ahmed, according to JURIST. Mohamud had removed Ahmed on November 4 and appointed Ibrahim Idle Suleiman in his place. The government rejected the ruling and swore in the new chief justice, Al Jazeera reported. Six Supreme Court judges, including Ahmed, have since filed a case against the government at the East African Court of Justice, according to Somali Guardian. Scandals, Nepotism and Allegations of State Capture Somalia scored 9 out of 100 in Transparency International’s 2025 Corruption Perceptions Index, published on February 10, 2026. It tied with South Sudan for the lowest score among 182 countries. The US State Department described corruption as pervasive across all sectors of the Somali government in its 2026 Investment Climate Statement. On January 7, 2026, the State Department suspended all aid programs that benefit the federal government. It alleged that Somali officials had destroyed a US-funded World Food Programme warehouse and seized 76 metric tons of food aid. Somalia’s foreign ministry denied the allegations and said work at Mogadishu’s port had not affected humanitarian aid. The United States later said it would resume WFP food distribution while it reviewed its other assistance, the Associated Press reported. On June 24, 2026, Kenyan immigration officers stopped Second Deputy Prime Minister Jibril Abdirashid Haji at Nairobi’s airport and sent him back to Mogadishu, amid reports that his Kenyan passport had been obtained by fraud, Ismail Abukar wrote in African Arguments. The same article said Mohamud disclosed in December 2022 that a biometric attendance system had found only 1,500 of more than 5,000 registered civil servants at work. In November 2025, Somali Guardian reported that Mohamud had suspended three senior presidential palace officials after unauthorized people were included in official delegations traveling abroad. Mohamud has also been accused of giving government posts to relatives. An opinion article WardheerNews published on April 16, 2026, said his son-in-law, Adam Roble, was appointed director-general of the Development and Reconstruction Bank on March 7, 2024. The author, Abdiqani Haji Abdi, also said a daughter of the president was made special adviser on foreign affairs in 2023 and a son was made commander of the Presidential Special Guard. Abdi called the appointments state capture. Saudi Arabia's Military Footprint in Somalia Raises Concerns Somalia and Saudi Arabia signed a military cooperation agreement in Riyadh on February 9, 2026. Neither country released details, Al Jazeera reported. Saudi Arabia is supporting a program to train 5,107 Somali soldiers at two camps in the Galgaduud region, Kenya’s The Standard reported , citing the Somali outlet Caasimada. In July 2026, Eastleigh Voice reported that media and military sources had accused Saudi Arabia of using foreign mercenaries from Romania, Ukraine, South Africa and Colombia as trainers. The outlet said the program would run for nine months and that about 2,000 recruits came from Somalia’s northeast. A Saudi military delegation inspected the camps in late June and early July 2026, according to an analysis Horn Review published in August. Regional outlets have linked the program to claims that Saudi Arabia is supporting recruitment for the war in Sudan, EU Reporter reported on September 15. In a decree issued Nov. 23, the Prime Minister's Office announced that Saadaq Joon would take over the Defence Ministry following Fiqi's departure from the position. advertisements The government did not specify why Fiqi left the ministry or announce whether he would be assigned another Cabinet position. Saadaq Joon, a member of Somalia's House of the People, previously served as commander of the Banadir Regional Police Force and has held several senior security positions. His appointment comes a day after Galmudug President Liibaan Ahmed Hassan announced a new regional Cabinet, following political changes in the central Somali state. According to political sources, Saadaq Joon's appointment is linked to a power-sharing arrangement between the federal government and former Galmudug President Ahmed Abdi Kaariye Qoorqoor following the election of Liibaan Ahmed Hassan. The reported arrangement is understood to involve the redistribution of senior government positions following the Galmudug leadership transition. However, the Prime Minister's Office did not publicly confirm that the defence appointment was part of a political agreement with Qoorqoor. The reshuffle also involved changes to two deputy ministerial positions. Ali Ifiye Ali was appointed deputy minister of ports and maritime transport, while Maryan Ali Abukar was named deputy minister of fisheries and the blue economy. The prime minister instructed the newly appointed officials to assume their responsibilities immediately and urged them to carry out their duties with integrity, dedication and accountability. Saadaq Joon takes over the Defence Ministry as Somalia continues military operations against al-Shabab and prepares to assume greater security responsibilities from African Union peacekeeping forces. The appointment also comes as the federal government and international partners discuss the future of the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM), whose current United Nations authorization expires Dec. 31. Fiqi had served as defence minister since April 2025, overseeing military operations against al-Shabab and cooperation with international security partners. President Mohamed Abdullahi Mohamed Report overlooks achievements registered by Somali Federal Government in addressing media freedom, gov't says Somalia's government on Thursday rejected a recent report of Amnesty International which says freedom of media has been deteriorating since President Mohamed Abdullahi Mohamed took office. “The report has overlooked the achievements registered by the Federal Government in challenging impunity, protecting journalists and addressing media freedom concerns in the past 3 years,” the Somali government said in a statement in response to the report. Amnesty's report said at least eight journalists have been killed since Mohamed took office in February 2017. “Somali journalists are under siege. From barely surviving explosive-wired cars, being shot, beaten up and arbitrarily arrested, journalists are working in horrifying conditions,” said Deprose Muchena, Amnesty International’s director for East and Southern Africa. Somali government said in response that it is “fully aware of its responsibility to protect the rights of every individual to liberty and security.” It added that the “majority of cases (53%) described in the report are not accurately media freedom cases and there is no single evidence to back this fabrication.” “The Federal Government vehemently denies and strongly disowns the allegations of bribery to the private media and views these ludicrous allegations as deliberate lies to misguide the public,” the statement added. Somalia, located in the Horn of Africa and bordered by Ethiopia to the west, the Gulf of Aden to the north had witnessed multiple terror attacks over the past two decades. Somali-based al-Qaeda affiliated group al-Shabaab has claimed responsibility for most of the attacks. somalia.summary: Somalia's government has rejected a recent report by Amnesty International that claims media freedom has worsened since President Mohamed Abdullahi Mohamed took office in 2017. The Somali government argues that the report fails to acknowledge the progress made in protecting journalists and addressing media freedom issues over the past three years. It highlights that at least eight journalists have been killed during this period, with Amnesty stating that Somali journalists face severe threats, including violence and arbitrary arrests. In response, the Somali government insists it is committed to safeguarding individual rights and disputes the accuracy of the report, claiming that many cases cited do not pertain to media freedom. The government also denies allegations of bribery involving private media, labeling them as falsehoods intended to mislead the public. Somalia has faced significant challenges, including terrorism, particularly from the al-Qaeda-affiliated group al-Shabaab, which has contributed to a precarious environment for journalists.

Posted by: Horseed Staff Madaxtooyada Soomaaliya ayaa war-saxaafadeed ka soo saartay kulan ay Magaalada Kampala ku yeesheen Madaxweynaha Jamhuuriyadda Uganda,… 23 November, 2026 Share Tweet Madaxtooyada Soomaaliya ayaa war-saxaafadeed ka soo saartay kulan ay Magaalada Kampala ku yeesheen Madaxweynaha Jamhuuriyadda Uganda, Yoweri Kaguta Museveni iyo Madaxweynaha Dowladda Federaalka Soomaaliya, Mudane Xasan Sheekh Maxamuud, 23-kii Nofembar 2026 booqasho rasmi ah oo hal maalin ah ku tagay Jamhuuriyadda Uganda. Labada Madaxweyne ayaa isdhaafsaday aragtiyo ku aaddan xaaladda siyaasadeed iyo tan amni ee Soomaaliya iyo gobolka. Waxay xoogga saareen baahida loo qabo in la ilaaliyo nabadda, amniga iyo xasilloonida Soomaaliya, Geeska Afrika iyo guud ahaan qaaradda Afrika. Waxay bogaadiyeen naf-hurka ay sameeyeen Ciidamada Difaaca Dadweynaha Uganda (UPDF) ee heshiiska laba-geesoodka ku jooga, Howlgalka Taageerada iyo Xasilinta Midowga Afrika ee Soomaaliya (AUSSOM), iyo Ciidamada Xoogga Dalka Soomaaliyeed (SNAF), kaalinta ay ka qaateen xasilinta dalka iyo la-dagaallanka Al-Shabaab. Madaxda ayaa adkeysay baahida loo qabo in la xoojiyo guulaha nabadeed iyo kuwa amni ee la gaaray tan iyo markii la bilaabay Howlgalka Taageerada iyo Xasilinta Midowga Afrika ee Soomaaliya (AUSSOM). Waxay sidoo kale adkeeyeen in lagu dhiso horumarkii ay gaareen howlgallada ka horreeyay, kuwaas oo kala ahaa Howlgalka Ku-meel-gaarka Midowga Afrika ee Soomaaliya (ATMIS) iyo Howlgalka Midowga Afrika ee Soomaaliya (AMISOM). Waxay kale oo ay ugu baaqeen in AUSSOM loo helo maalgelin ku filan, la saadaalin karo oo waarta. Madaxda ayaa xusay go’aannadii lagu gaaray Shirka Madaxeed ee labaad ee aan caadiga ahayn iyo kulamadii ka horreeyay ee Wasiirrada Gaashaandhigga iyo Taliyeyaasha Ciidamada ee dalalka ciidamada ku leh AUSSOM iyo Jamhuuriyadda Federaalka Soomaaliya. Shirkaas waxaa 31-kii Luulyo 2026 lagu qabtay Speke Resort Munyonyo, Kampala, Uganda, waxaana shirguddoominayay Madaxweynaha Jamhuuriyadda Uganda, Mudane Yoweri K. Museveni. Labada hoggaamiye ayaa muujiyey baahida loo qabo in Dowladda Federaalka Soomaaliya, Dowlad Goboleedyada Xubnaha ka ah iyo dhammaan saamileyda ay xiriirkooda kor u qaadaan. Arrintaas waxaa loo marayaa dib-u-heshiisiin, xoojinta maamul wanaagga iyo nabad-dhisid, si loo xaqiijiyo amniga, xasilloonida iyo horumarka dhaqaale ee dalka oo dhan iyadoo Madaxweynaha Uganda uu hawlo dhexdhexaadin ah u imaan doono Magaalada Muqdisho. somalia.content: The Grandchild Deficit Of Somalia: The Political Class Never Leaves Anything Behind - OpEd - Eurasia Review Monday, November 23, 2026 Eurasia Review A Journal of Analysis and News News Africa East Asia Pacific The Americas Europe Middle East South and Central Asia Analysis Opinion Business GDKP Social Religion Entertainment Book Reviews Environment Technology Science Health About Eurasia Review Eurasia Review’s Editorial Staff Authors and Partners Submit an Article Privacy Policy And Terms Of Use Contact Subscribe to Eurasia Review Photo Credit: Kremena Koleva, Pexels Opinion 1 Africa Social Issues The Grandchild Deficit Of Somalia: The Political Class Never Leaves Anything Behind – OpEd November 23, 2026 November 23, 2026 Dr. Suleiman Walhad 0 Comments By Dr. Suleiman Walhad Key Takeaways: Somalia’s 4.5 clan power-sharing system and reliance on foreign aid create incentives for politicians to prioritise short-term patronage and personal enrichment over long-term public goods such as schools, hospitals and infrastructure. Because political survival depends on clan brokers rather than voters and because leaders can rely on second passports and overseas services for their own families, multi-decade nation-building projects are treated as career risks. The article argues that the resulting cycle of donor conferences, evaporated funds and postponed development will continue until Somali politicians must answer to citizens at home and send their own children to the institutions they claim to build. If you ever find yourself wandering through the hallways of power in Mogadishu, or any regional capital, town, or village across Somalia, you might notice a curious architectural omission. There are plenty of reinforced concrete blast walls, shiny tinted-window Land Cruisers, and VIP airport lounges. What you will not find anywhere in the country, however, is a single blueprint for a pediatric hospital, a public high school, or a modest commuter train. To the untrained eye, this looks like an oversight. Surely, any normal human being handed the keys to a nation, along with billions of dollars in international goodwill, would think, “You know what would be really neat? If my grandchildren didn’t have to fly to Nairobi or Istanbul or Dubai or India where many never return from, every time they got a toothache or pain in the stomach.” However, in the grand theater of Somali politics, thinking about your grandchildren is treated like a dangerous radicalism. Why build a legacy for 2050 when you can barely survive the parliamentary no-confidence vote scheduled for next Tuesday? That is assuming, of course, that 2050 ever crosses the political class’s mind at all. To understand why Somalia’s political class treats nation-building like an allergic reaction, one has to appreciate the sheer genius of the 4.5 power-sharing formula. Invented as a temporary bandage in the year 2000, the 4.5 system divides political power among four major clans and a half-share for everyone else. In theory, it was meant to keep the peace. In practice, it turned the Somali state into a giant, rotating buffet where every clan takes turns loading up their plates before the kitchen catches fire. Under this system, a politician does not win office by promising voters better roads, cleaner water, public schools, or healthcare centers, nor any grand national project, for that matter. Voters do not actually get a vote. Instead, aspiring leaders spend small fortunes, often bankrolled by meddling foreign powers invested in keeping Somalia weak and ungoverned, to bribe a handful of clan elders and political brokers inside heavily guarded hotel compounds. Once seated in parliament or a cabinet ministry, the newly minted statesman confronts an immediate, existential truth: he does not work for the Somali public. He works for the cousins who put him there, who expect their return on investment by Friday, and for his own bank account, funding a four-year lifestyle of unchecked luxury. Building a highway takes ten years. Laying railway tracks across the Horn of Africa takes a generation. Handing out a lucrative no-bid catering contract to your uncle, however, takes fifteen minutes and a rubber stamp. When your political life expectancy is roughly that of a housefly in a windstorm, multi-decade infrastructure projects are not just unattractive, they are career suicide. Why plant a tree whose shade you will never sit under when you can chop down the sapling and sell it for firewood right now? And right there, in that short-sighted calculation, is why grandchildren never even enter the mind of Somalia’s political class. What a shame! Of course, this whole enterprise would run out of steam fairly quickly if politicians actually had to fund it by taxing the local population. Taxation is terribly inconvenient; when citizens pay taxes, they develop the annoying habit of asking where the money went. Thankfully, the international community has spent decades sparing Somali leaders from this awkwardness by showering the country with foreign grants, donor conferences, and humanitarian aid. In truth, some of those funds were never meant to build anything at all, but rather to keep the nation floating in the ether, perpetually half-alive, dependent, and going nowhere. In the eyes of the political elite, foreign aid is not a lifeline meant to help Somalia stand on its own two feet; it is a magical, renewable ATM bankrolled either by guilty Western diplomats or by newly wealthy foreign powers eager to flex their geopolitical muscles at the expense of a defenseless, weakened nation. The routine has been perfected into a high art form. Step one: attend a glamorous donor summit in Brussels or London, or some other shiny foreign capital with better hotels and functioning hospitals, deliver a tear-jerking speech about resilience and state-building, and pose for photos. Step two: fly home with pledges of millions of dollars for capacity building and institutional reform. Step three: watch a mysterious percentage of those funds evaporate into thin air somewhere between the central bank and a fictitious consultancy firm registered in a neighboring country. When donors inevitably ask why not a single brick has been laid, why there is no classroom for tomorrow’s students, no clinic for future patients, not even a mile of railway track for the next generation, the political class suddenly performs an extraordinary display of theatrical bewilderment. A railway? A school? A clinic? In this security climate? Surely, such ambitions are unrealistic! And just like that, the conversation shifts. Development is postponed, accountability is buried beneath the language of security, and the money is quietly redirected towards urgent stabilization efforts, which, rather conveniently, seem to have an endless appetite for more Land Cruisers. Apparently, the roads to development can wait. The roads for the convoys cannot. Perhaps the most crucial secret to this carefree governance is the ultimate escape hatch: the second passport. It is a running joke among ordinary Somalis that the true capital of Somalia is not Mogadishu, Garowe, or Hargeisa, but rather London, Minneapolis, Toronto, Stockholm or Doha, Dubai, and now Istanbul. When a minister’s own children attend pristine public schools in Virginia, and his grandchildren are born in state-of-the-art hospitals in Ontario, the lack of functioning clinics in Baidoa feels less like a national tragedy and more like an abstract academic problem. Why lose sleep over Somalia’s crumbling education system when your own family’s tuition is already paid in Canadian dollars? And so the cycle spins on. The speeches grow grander, donor conferences more frequent, and four-wheel drives ever shinier. Meanwhile, schools remain unbuilt, hospitals chronically underfunded, and phantom railways safely confined to PowerPoint presentations. Perhaps the cycle will only break when institutions begin to function, when Somali politicians are compelled to earn their votes from citizens in the place of the political networks built on divided and multiple loyalties, and when those in power are willing to send their own grandchildren to the very schools they claim to fund. Until then, the only thing being built in Mogadishu is another exit strategy. About Dr. Suleiman Walhad Dr. Suleiman Walhad writes on the Horn of Africa economies and politics. somalia.summary: In Somalia, the political class prioritizes short-term gains over long-term development, resulting in a "grandchild deficit." The 4.5 clan power-sharing system incentivizes politicians to focus on immediate patronage and personal enrichment rather than investing in essential public goods like schools and hospitals. Political survival hinges on clan loyalty rather than voter support, leading to a neglect of nation-building efforts. Foreign aid, rather than being a means to foster independence, has become a tool for maintaining a weak state, with funds often disappearing before they can be utilized for development. Politicians, who often send their families abroad for education and healthcare, lack motivation to improve local institutions. The cycle of donor conferences and unfulfilled promises continues, with real accountability only possible when politicians are compelled to serve their constituents and invest in the future of their own children. Until then, Somalia's infrastructure remains underdeveloped, and the political elite's focus remains on immediate personal benefits.

الجولة الخامسة المؤجلة من الدوري الرواندي. وقرر مدرب الفريق جوزيف زينباور خوض اللقاء بدلًا من تأجيله، ليجعله بروفة ختامية قبل مواجهة حوريا كوناكري الغيني يوم الأحد 29 نوفمبر على ملعب "أماهورو"، في عن أجواء المنافسات الرسمية. ومن المتوقع أن يستعين زينباور بالعناصر التالية: حراسة المرمى: سفيان فريد خط الدفاع: مصطفى كرشوم، بابي ديارا، إرنست لوزولو، ياسر عوض خط الوسط: محمد راوا، ولي الدين خضر، عبد الرواندي ويعدّ مدرب الهلال السوداني الذي يقضي موسمه الأول مع النادي الأزرق، عددًا من البدلاء لتجهيزهم لماراثون المباريات الشاق الذي ينتظر الفريق، إذ سيخوض 3 مواجهات في المرحلة الأولى من مجموعات دوري أبطال أفريقيا، بالتزامن مع منافسات قوية في الدوري الرواندي. ويطمح الفريق إلى تحقيق مكاسب مضاعفة من مباراته المقبلة، تتمثل في اعتلاء صدارة الدوري بنسخته الجديدة، ومنح نجومه دفعة معنوية كبيرة قبل خوض مواجهته المرتقبة ضد الفريق الغيني في مستهل مشواره القاري. وتنطلق مباراة الهلال السوداني ضد كييفو في الساعة 7:30 بتوقيت مكة المكرمة (الساعة 6:30 بالتوقيت المحلي في رواندا)، وستنقل المباراة عبر منصات المحلي محمد عطا. اقرأ أيضًا الهلال السوداني يقيل أويرورو ويعين مدربا فرنسيا خلفا له الهلال يخطف فوزًا ثمينًا من البوليس ويقترب من صدارة الدوري الرواندي واتخذت الإدارة قرار تغيير الجهاز الفني دون النظر الهلال السوداني على إعداد الفريق الرديف عبر معسكر تجريبي طويل خاض خلاله مباريات ودية قوية، وعززت صفوفه بنخبة من النجوم والمحترفين الأجانب لضمان تأهله إلى المرحلة الختامية من المسابقة التي سيشارك فيها السوداني لحساب الجولة الثانية من دور المجموعات. كما سيستقبل المغرب الفاسي فريق حوريا كوناكري يوم 19 دجنبر، ضمن الجولة الثالثة، في مواجهتين يراهن عليهما ممثل الكرة المغربية لتحقيق نتائج إيجابية وجمع football.summary: أعلن نادي الهلال السوداني عن تعيين المدرب الفرنسي ألكسندر لافيت لتولي مسؤولية تدريب فريق الرديف والفئات السنية بالنادي. يمتد عقد لافيت لمدة موسمين، حيث سيتولى الإشراف على تطوير اللاعبين الشباب. جاء هذا الإعلان عبر الحساب الرسمي للنادي، الذي رحب بالمدرب الجديد وتمنى له التوفيق في مهمته. يُذكر أن لافيت، البالغ من العمر 29 عامًا، لديه خبرة سابقة في تدريب فرق شبابية، حيث عمل مع باريس سان جيرمان وأيضًا كمدير فني لفريق ستاد أبيدجان الإيفواري. خلال فترة تدريبه في أبيدجان، واجه الأهلي المصري مرتين في دوري أبطال أفريقيا، حيث خسر في كلا المباراتين. يُعتبر هذا التعيين خطوة جديدة في مسيرة الهلال السوداني لتعزيز قدراته في تطوير المواهب الشابة.
